paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Boredom is a curious mixture of restlessness and lethargy. People who are bored fidget, check the time and find that their attention keeps drifting, yet at the same time they feel tired and slow, as if the hours themselves had become heavy. For a long time psychologists paid it little attention, treating it as a trivial mood rather than a subject for serious study. That has changed. In 2012, a team led by John Eastwood of York University in Toronto proposed a definition that is now widely used: boredom is 'the aversive experience of wanting, but being unable, to engage in satisfying activity'. In other words, the problem is not simply that there is nothing to do, but that nothing we can do feels worth doing.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Many people, it seems, will go to remarkable lengths to escape it. In a series of studies published in 2014, the psychologist Timothy Wilson and his colleagues at the University of Virginia asked volunteers to sit alone in a plain room for between six and fifteen minutes with nothing to do except think. Most reported that they found the experience unpleasant. In one version of the study, participants could press a button that gave them a mild electric shock, which all of them had earlier said they would pay money to avoid. Even so, 67 per cent of the men and 25 per cent of the women chose to shock themselves at least once rather than sit quietly with their thoughts.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: James Danckert, a neuroscientist at the University of Waterloo in Canada, argues that boredom is better understood as a signal than as a problem. In the same way that pain warns us to take our hand away from something hot, boredom tells us that what we are doing is not meeting our needs and that we should change course. Seen in this light, the feeling has a purpose. The difficulty, Danckert suggests, is that we often respond to the signal badly, reaching for the quickest distraction instead of asking what we actually want to do. His interest in the subject grew partly out of research with patients recovering from brain injuries, many of whom reported feeling bored far more often than they had before.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: That quick distraction is now always within reach. A generation ago, waiting for a bus or standing in a queue meant a few minutes with nothing to occupy the mind. Today most people fill those moments by looking at a phone. Some researchers worry that this habit makes boredom harder to bear when it does arrive, because we have had so little practice in tolerating it. Others point out that people who are frequently bored are more likely to report overeating, risky behaviour and difficulty concentrating, although it is not clear whether boredom causes these problems or simply accompanies them. Researchers are also divided on whether constant access to entertainment makes people more easily bored in general, or simply changes the way they spend the gaps in their day.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Boredom can also be costly at work. Jobs that involve watching for rare events, such as checking security screens or monitoring machinery, are notoriously difficult to perform well for long periods, because attention fades when nothing happens. Employers have tried various ways of reducing the problem: rotating staff between different tasks during a shift, building short breaks into the working day and giving workers more control over the order in which they complete their duties. Some schools have taken a similar approach, breaking long lessons into shorter activities so that pupils' attention is renewed.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Yet boredom may have an unexpected benefit. In a study published in 2014, Sandi Mann and Rebekah Cadman of the University of Central Lancashire asked one group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a deliberately dull task. All the participants were then asked to think of as many uses as they could for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had done the copying came up with more ideas than a control group that had gone straight to the creative task. A third group, who had only had to read the directory rather than copy from it, did better still. Mann suggests that undemanding activities allow the mind to wander, and that this daydreaming gives people the chance to make new connections between ideas.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: None of this means that boredom should be welcomed without question. Eastwood warns that it would be a mistake to assume that every dull afternoon will lead to a burst of creativity; boredom is useful only when it prompts us to look for something more meaningful to do. Danckert agrees that the feeling is worth listening to rather than silencing at once. The challenge for most of us, it seems, is not to avoid boredom altogether, but to stay with it long enough to hear what it is telling us.
